narrative.episodeSummary: A 34-year-old female with a history of similar self-terminating episodes presented with palpitations. Vitals showed a heart rate of 190 bpm, stable blood pressure (118/76 mmHg), and normal oxygen saturation (98%). ECG revealed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 190 bpm, no clear P waves, and no ST deviation. Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) were within normal limits. Troponin was negative. The episode was captured and classified as stable supraventricular tachycardia.
narrative.clinicalContext: The patient experienced an episode of regular narrow-complex tachycardia (supraventricular tachycardia) characterized by a rapid heart rate (190 bpm) and hemodynamic stability. The ECG showed a regular rhythm, narrow QRS complexes, and absence of clear P waves. The event occurred after consuming caffeine.
narrative.mostLikelyEtiology: The most likely etiology is caffeine-induced paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), possibly atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) or atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT), given the abrupt onset, narrow QRS morphology, and history of similar episodes.
contributingFactors: History of prior similar self-terminating episodes
uncertaintyAndMissingData: Specific type of SVT (e.g., AVNRT vs AVRT) cannot be definitively determined without further investigation (e.g., adenosine challenge, electrophysiology study).
